panel_trend.remember: Is each market above or below its long-run average, and is that average rising?
panel_trend.plain: One word per market: Bull, Flat or Bear, from a fixed 200-day rule. It describes the trend; it does not predict it. Tested as a trading switch, it cut losses in crashes but earned less (F22).

provenance.from: Daily closing prices: SPY, IEF, GLD, UUP from Tiingo (refreshed Sundays), Bitcoin from Coinbase hourly candles
provenance.updated: computed each time the page loads

panel_lineage.remember: The family tree of strategies we chose to track, and how far each has been promoted.
panel_lineage.plain: Each strategy started as one optimizer result. Promotion needs evidence: a strategy rejected by the adversary can never move past 'backtest winner'. 'Forward test' means it is being watched on new data, which promotes nothing.

provenance.updated: when a strategy is registered, promoted or marked

panel_decay.remember: An alarm that fires if a strategy starts doing worse than it did when it was tested.
panel_decay.plain: For each watched strategy, every new trade is compared with the trades from its test period. A running score (CUSUM) falls when results are below that baseline; crossing -3 is the alert.

provenance.from: Backtests on new candles, or TradingView paper trades if any

panel_jobs.remember: The collector's to-do list: what ran, when, and whether it worked.
panel_jobs.plain: Each line is a scheduled task. 'ok' means it finished; 'failed' shows the error on hover; 'overdue' means it should have run more than two hours ago. The newest crypto candle shows the collector is alive.

panel_candidates.remember: Every strategy setting the optimizer ever tried, with the adversary's verdict on the best ones.
panel_candidates.plain: Thousands of random settings were tested on old data. A few looked good; the adversary then attacked them. Failures are never deleted, because the number of tries is what tells us how lucky the best one probably was.

provenance.updated: the adversary weekly; the optimizer only when run

panel_report.remember: The adversary's nine attacks on one candidate, with its profit curve.
panel_report.plain: Click a reported candidate to see whether it survived each attack, and its account value and drawdown over its test windows. One hard attack landing means REJECTED.

provenance.from: forge.db adversarial_reports, plus the engine re-running the candidate on its pinned windows

panel_screen.remember: A ranking of the 50 most-traded US funds by how smoothly they rose over a year.
panel_screen.plain: Each fund's 12-month return divided by how much it swung. A ranking, not a signal: momentum tested on funds found no edge (F20). The top-50 list itself is re-chosen weekly by trading volume.

provenance.from: Daily prices: Alpaca (screen funds) and Tiingo (research funds); fund list from Tiingo's ticker list and Alpaca
provenance.updated: list Sundays 23:00 UTC, ranking Mondays 06:00 UTC

panel_patterns.remember: 52 old market sayings, each tested once on real data, with the verdict kept.
panel_patterns.plain: Sayings like 'sell in May' or 'don't fight the Fed', written down before testing and never removed. None proved out; five were suggestive, about what luck gives (F18).

provenance.from: Prices from Tiingo; economic data from the US Treasury, CBOE, BLS and NY Fed, each value dated when it was released

panel_context.remember: The economy's dashboard lights: fear gauge, interest rates, credit stress, valuation.
panel_context.plain: Each line is one widely watched series with a plain status word. Context only: none of them may trigger a trade, and the classic readings of most of them were tested and not established (F18).

provenance.from: CBOE (VIX, put/call), FRED (yields, credit spreads, Sahm rule, fed funds), Shiller (CAPE), and SPY's own prices

panel_insider.remember: Company bosses buying their own company's stock, from their legal filings.
panel_insider.plain: Executives and directors must report their trades to the SEC on Form 4 within two days. A 'cluster' is several of them buying at once. Untested here: it may say nothing about what the price does next.

provenance.from: SEC Form 4 filings, collected by the Edgar Alert project

panel_tracker.remember: Today's big US companies you or a screen chose to watch, with their key numbers.
panel_tracker.plain: Price changes, valuation ratios and financial-health scores for S&P 100 names, each with how it ranks among the 100 and within its industry. Facts and traditional readings, not recommendations.

provenance.from: S&P 100 list from Wikipedia; prices from Alpaca; company financials from SEC filings (XBRL company facts)

panel_autopsy.remember: A plain record of each new trade the two forward tests made, and the conditions at the time.
panel_autopsy.plain: Shows the market mood, weekday and outcome of each forward trade. Descriptive only: picking strategies from what winners had in common is a known trap, so nothing is built from this table.

provenance.from: The same forward trades the decay monitor uses
provenance.updated: computed when the page loads, cached until a new candle

panel_paper.remember: Does the live TradingView alert match what our own backtest engine would have done?
panel_paper.plain: Each TradingView alert is a pretend (paper) trade. This table checks the alert's price and timing against the engine's. Mismatches mean the live version and the tested version have drifted apart.

provenance.from: TradingView alerts relayed by davesbridge (signals.db, read-only), and engine re-runs

panel_glossary.remember: Every term on this page, in one line each.
panel_glossary.plain: Click any (i) button for the full entry; this list has them all, A to Z.

backtest.remember: Replaying a strategy on old prices to see what it would have done.
backtest.plain: Useful but easy to fool: try enough settings and one will look brilliant by luck. That is why every backtest here is attacked before anyone believes it.

is.remember: The older data a strategy was chosen on: its practice exam.
is.plain: Results here are flattering by construction, because the settings were picked to do well on exactly this data.

oos.remember: Newer data the strategy never saw while being chosen: its real exam.
oos.plain: A strategy that only works in-sample learned noise. The out-of-sample result is the one that counts.

forward_test.remember: Watching a strategy on data that did not exist when it was chosen.
forward_test.plain: The cleanest evidence there is, but slow: it takes as long as the trades take to happen. Three are running here; none may be re-tuned while it runs.

pre_registration.remember: Writing down the test and its pass mark before looking at the answer.
pre_registration.plain: Stops us from moving the goalposts after seeing results. Every study here is registered, approved by you, then run once.

buy_and_hold.remember: Just owning the thing and doing nothing. The benchmark every strategy must beat.
buy_and_hold.plain: If a clever rule earns less than simply holding, the rule is costing money. Nothing in this project has beaten buy-and-hold yet.

sharpe.remember: Reward per unit of bumpiness: how much you earned for the ups and downs you sat through.
sharpe.plain: Average return divided by how much returns swing. Higher is better; above 1 a year is good for a whole portfolio. 'SR/trade' is the same idea per trade.

psr.remember: How sure we can be the true Sharpe is above zero, given how few results we have.
psr.plain: Goes from 0 to 1. Our usual bar is 0.95: about a 1-in-20 chance the result is luck. Fewer trades or wild results lower it.

dsr.remember: PSR after allowing for how many strategies were tried: 'is this better than the luckiest of N random tries?'
dsr.plain: The adversary's key test (A2). Needs 0.95 to pass. More tries raise the bar, which is why failures are never deleted.

p_value.remember: The chance of seeing a result this strong if nothing real were going on.
p_value.plain: Small is good: 0.01 means 1 in 100. With many tests, some small ones happen by luck, so the bar is divided by the number of tests (see Bonferroni).

bonferroni.remember: Ten lottery tickets win more often than one: so with ten tests, demand ten times stronger proof.
bonferroni.plain: The pass mark is divided by the number of tests. 40 tests at 0.05 means each needs p below 0.00125.

drawdown.remember: The drop from a peak to the lowest point before a new high: the worst stretch you sat through.
drawdown.plain: A 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain to get back. 'Max drawdown' is the worst one in the period.

cagr.remember: The steady yearly growth rate that would turn the starting amount into the ending amount.
cagr.plain: Compound annual growth rate. It hides the bumps: two strategies with the same CAGR can have very different drawdowns.

basis_point.remember: One hundredth of one percent: 100 bp = 1%.
basis_point.plain: Used for small differences: a 5 bp daily edge is 0.05% a day.

survivorship.remember: Studying only the winners that are still around, and forgetting the ones that died.
survivorship.plain: Today's S&P 100 contains only companies that succeeded. Testing on that list flatters any strategy, so backtests use a list of who was in the index at each past date.

percentile.remember: Where a value ranks: 80 means higher than 80% of the others.
percentile.plain: In the Tracker, the first small number is the rank among the S&P 100, the second among companies in the same industry.

ttm.remember: The last four quarters added up: a rolling year.
ttm.plain: Used for profits and sales so every company is measured over a full, recent year, whatever its fiscal calendar.

sic.remember: The government's industry code for a company, used to compare it with its peers.
sic.plain: Standard Industrial Classification, from the company's SEC registration. Two-digit groups such as 35 (machinery and computers) are used here.

col_id.plain: Each optimizer result gets one; reports and lineage refer to it.

col_pair.remember: What was traded, e.g. BTC-USD (bitcoin priced in dollars) or SPY.
col_pair.plain: Crypto pairs trade around the clock; funds only in market hours.

col_tf.remember: How long each price bar is: 1h is hourly, 1d is daily.
col_tf.plain: Shorter bars mean more trades and more costs.

col_family.remember: The kind of strategy: each family is one trading idea with adjustable settings.
col_family.plain: smrt_v41 (a multi-indicator trend system), core (simpler trend), squeeze (breakouts after quiet periods).

col_verdict.remember: The adversary's ruling: SURVIVED, FRAGILE or REJECTED.
col_verdict.plain: REJECTED: a hard attack (A1, A2 or A6) landed. FRAGILE: two or more soft ones. SURVIVED: at most one soft one, which only earns paper trading. Every candidate so far is REJECTED.

col_wf.remember: Did it make money in most separate time slices, or just one lucky stretch?
col_wf.plain: The share of walk-forward folds that were profitable (attack A3).

col_plateau.remember: Do nearby settings work too? Good strategies sit on a plateau, not a spike.
col_plateau.plain: Share of small setting nudges that keep the result (attack A4). Low means the exact settings were luck.

col_mc_dd95.remember: A bad-luck worst case: the drawdown you would hit in 1 of 20 shuffled histories.
col_mc_dd95.plain: Monte Carlo: the trades are reshuffled thousands of times; this is the 95th-percentile drawdown (attack A8).

col_n.remember: How many trades in the practice and real-exam periods.
col_n.plain: Below about 30, any result is mostly noise (attack A1).

col_pf.remember: Money won divided by money lost. Above 1 makes money; 1.5 is good.
col_pf.plain: Shown for in-sample and out-of-sample separately.

col_net.remember: Profit in dollars in the out-of-sample period, on a $10,000 test account.

col_gate.remember: Did it pass the optimizer's first, simple filter (enough trades, PF above a floor)?
col_gate.plain: 1 = passed. Passing the gate only earns an adversary report.

A1.remember: Too few trades to tell skill from luck.
A1.plain: Hard attack: fewer out-of-sample trades than a statistical floor means REJECTED.

A2.remember: Is this better than the luckiest of all the random strategies we tried?
A2.plain: Hard attack: DSR below 0.95 means REJECTED. Every candidate so far has failed here.

A3.remember: Does it work in most separate stretches of time?
A3.plain: Soft attack: too few profitable folds.

A4.remember: Does it still work if the settings are nudged 10-25%?
A4.plain: Soft attack: a result that collapses when nudged was tuned to noise.

A5.remember: Does the edge survive if trading costs double?

A6.remember: Does it get better if trades are filled later? That means it is cheating with the future.
A6.plain: Hard attack: real edges get worse when delayed, not better.

A7.remember: Does the idea work on other markets too?
A7.plain: Soft attack: no other pair reaches a profit factor of 1.1.

A8.remember: Would bad luck produce a drop bigger than the risk budget?
A8.plain: Soft attack, from the Monte Carlo shuffle.

A9.remember: Did all the profit come from one kind of market, such as one bull run?

st_hypothesis.remember: Registered for tracking; no evidence attached yet.
st_hypothesis.plain: The bottom of the promotion ladder.

st_backtest_winner.remember: Looked good in a backtest. As far as a rejected strategy can ever go.
st_backtest_winner.plain: Promotion past this needs the adversary's SURVIVED verdict.

st_oos_validated.remember: Survived the adversary on its out-of-sample data.
st_oos_validated.plain: Licence to paper-trade, not to trade.

st_paper_validated.remember: Matched its backtest in live paper trading over enough time.
st_paper_validated.plain: Needs about 30 reconciled trades over 60 days.

st_approved.remember: A human decision. Code can never set it.

st_retired.remember: No longer watched; its history is kept.
st_retired.plain: Its history and all its trials stay on record, so they keep counting.

cusum.remember: A running tally of 'worse than expected' that triggers an alert at -3.
cusum.plain: Cumulative sum: each forward trade adds how far it was above or below the baseline; good trades pull it back up to 0. Slow but steady: it needs dozens of trades.

baseline.remember: What a strategy's trades looked like in its test period: the yardstick for new trades.
baseline.plain: The decay monitor compares new trades against it.

vol_adj.remember: Return per unit of bumpiness over a year: smooth risers score high.

volatility.remember: How much the price swings, as a yearly percentage.
volatility.plain: About 15-20% for the stock market, 50%+ for bitcoin.

reversal_flag.remember: Up or down a lot in the last month: big short moves often partly reverse.
reversal_flag.plain: Flags the top and bottom 10% by 1-month return.

dollar_vol_rank.remember: Rank by how many dollars change hands each day: 1 is the most traded.
dollar_vol_rank.plain: Median of the last 20 trading days.

cash_like.remember: A fund that barely moves (T-bills), so return per swing means nothing for it; ranked last.

stale.remember: This price is more than a few days old.
stale.plain: The data feed for it may have stopped; treat the number with care.

pat_supported.remember: Held up after correcting for testing 52 sayings at once, in both halves of history.

pat_suggestive.remember: Pointed the right way, but not strongly enough to rule out luck.
pat_suggestive.plain: Five of 52, about what luck alone would give.

pat_not_supported.remember: The data did not back the saying.
pat_not_supported.plain: Most of the 52 sayings ended here.

pat_opposite.remember: The data pointed the other way, strongly.
pat_opposite.plain: One saying ended here: the data pointed against it.

pat_too_few.remember: Not enough separate occasions to test.
pat_too_few.plain: Usually a rare event, such as a recession signal, with only a handful of past cases.

pat_on_now.plain: Context only, never a trading rule.

pat_windows.remember: How many separate, non-overlapping occasions were tested.
pat_windows.plain: Eight windows can only say so much.

ins_cluster.remember: Two or more insiders buying the same company's stock within days.
ins_cluster.plain: The classic claim is that this means they see good news. Untested here.

ins_open_market.remember: An insider paying their own money for shares on the exchange (Form 4 code P).
ins_open_market.plain: Unlike awards or option exercises, it costs them cash.

ins_form4.remember: The SEC filing an insider must make within two business days of a trade.
ins_form4.plain: Its date of filing can be later than the trade itself; the screens use the trade date.

regime.remember: The day's market mood: trend_up, trend_down or chop (going sideways).
regime.plain: From the previous day's 50-day average slope and the ADX trend-strength reading (below 20 = chop).

vix_band.remember: How nervous the stock market was that day, compared with the past year: <50, 50-90 or >90.
vix_band.plain: The VIX's percentile over the last 252 trading days.

hold_h.remember: How many hours the trade was open.
hold_h.plain: From the fill at entry to the exit, or to now if the trade is still open.

alert_price.remember: The price TradingView reported vs the price our engine used.

engine_fired.remember: Whether our engine would have signalled the same trade at that moment.
engine_fired.plain: 'no' means the live and tested versions disagree.

rolling_pf.remember: Profit factor over the last 30 days of paper trades.
rolling_pf.plain: Needs about 1.2 over 30+ trades to count.

bull.remember: Price above its 200-day average, and the average rising.
bull.plain: A rising market by this rule.

bear.remember: Price below its 200-day average, and the average falling.
bear.plain: A falling market by this rule.

flat.remember: Price and average disagree, or the average is level: no clear trend.
flat.plain: Treasuries flipped in and out of this state ten times in a year, which shows how noisy one reading can be.

sma200.remember: The average closing price of the last 200 trading days: the long-run trend line.
sma200.plain: Crypto uses 200 calendar days, since it trades every day.

percentile_change.remember: How much the price changed over the last month or year.
percentile_change.plain: Total return over 21 or 252 trading days, dividends included (adjusted prices).

pat_statuses.remember: The verdict each saying got when tested: SUPPORTED, SUGGESTIVE, NOT SUPPORTED, OPPOSITE or TOO FEW.
pat_statuses.plain: Click the (i) beside each status word for what it means. No saying reached SUPPORTED.
